title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 Why Causal Inference?
Sound causal reasoning is essential to pharmacometrics (Rogers, Maas, and Pitarch (2023)). A motivating premise of this book is that pharmacometricians will be better able to engage in causal reasoning with stochastic data if they are able to avail themselves of the formal vocabulary, notation, and concepts of formal causal inference. While this book may introduce the reader to some new analytic techniques, our emphasis will be on causal concepts as an aid to elicitation and interpretation, as suggested in the figure below.
Our perspective is that causal reasoning is especially important in pharmacometrics because it is often the case that pharmacometric questions must be addressed without the benefit of a dedicated randomized trial. As such, our goal is often not to provide the gold standard evidence that would result from a randomized trial, but rather to foster high-quality decision making when the ideal data is not available at the time the decision needs to be made, as suggested in the following figure.

title: 2  Causal Directed Acyclic Graphs
text:
2.1 What is a Causal DAG?
First, a distinction: the Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) discussed here will be specifically causal DAGs which, as the name suggests, convey causal information. In principle, DAGs can also be used to convey non-causal information (e.g. they are sometimes used to specify hierarchical models, which may or may not have causal interpretability), but in the context of this book, a “DAG” can always be understood to have causal semantics attached to it.
In the context of causal inference, DAGs consist of nodes, representing variables, and “directed edges” (a.k.a. arrows), representing causal dependencies between the variables. A proper DAG will contain only unidirectional arrows and will not contain directed loops (“acyclic”), corresponding to the notion that there can be no instantaneous causal feedback (feedback in general can be represented, but it must proceed in a temporal sequence). You will (very soon) see DAGs that seemingly violate this requirement of directedness by including bi-directional arrows. However, as will soon be explained, bi-directional arrows are only to be understood as a notational shortcut, not as a representation of instantaneous feedback.

title: 2  Causal Directed Acyclic Graphs
text:
2.2 DAG conventions in this book
Our graphical conventions in this book are intended to be similar to those used in the popular “dagitty” web application (Textor et al. (2016)), but with some modifications to better support readers who are red-green colorblind. The conventions we will use are:

The pathway(s) of causal dependence that we wish to quantify will be shown in blue (whereas in dagitty they show in green).
We won’t graphically distinguish between treatment nodes, outcome nodes, and other nodes. However, the previous convention makes it clear how to identify the treatment and outcome nodes, but determining where the blue arrows originate and terminate.
Biasing pathways (or unblocked “backdoor paths” to use the technical term that we will discuss later) will be shown in red.
Adjusted variables (variables that we control for in our analyses) will be depicted with rectangle-shaped nodes.
Causal dependencies that are neither biasing nor of direct interest will be depicted in gray (or “grey”, if you prefer).
Dashed lines to represent potential causal dependencies of a more speculative nature.

section: 2.3 Examples of DAGs in Drug Development
text:
2.3 Examples of DAGs in Drug Development

2.3.1 Randomized Controlled Trial
This is probably the simplest and most common DAG describing the effect of an intervention, here the treatment \(D\), on an outcome or response \(R\). An intervention is a factor that can be actively manipulated to elicit a change in the outcome.
Examples of intervention are: dose, rescue medication; counter-example: race.









In this 2nd DAG, we see the data generation model corresponding to an RCT with precision covariate L. For instance, L can be a stratification factor. If L is expected to have a clear effect on R, it is sometimes referred to as a precision covariate. Please note the absence of arrow between L and D. Absence of arrow is synonym for absence of causal relationship.











2.3.2 Common D-E-R DAGs
In pharmacometrics, a common causal structure links dose \(D\) to an exposure metric \(E\) (e.g. AUC or \(C_\text{max}\)) and then to a response \(R\). The following DAGs illustrate three important variants of this structure.
In the simplest case, the effect of \(D\) on \(R\) is fully mediated by \(E\). A mediator is a node on the pathway between intervention and outcome. Full mediation is a strong assumption.









A direct path from \(D\) to \(R\) (bypassing \(E\)) can be added to capture effects not mediated through the measured exposure. The total causal effect of \(D\) on \(R\) then decomposes as: \[\text{Total effect} = \text{Direct effect } (D \to R) + \text{Indirect effect } (D \to E \to R).\] This distinction matters in practice: when the measured exposure (e.g. plasma AUC) is a poor proxy for exposure at the site of action — such as the brain or lungs — the D-to-E-to-R path alone may not capture the full effect of dose on response. In such settings, estimating the total effect of \(D\) on \(R\) directly is a more robust target.









When a covariate \(L\) affects both \(E\) and \(R\), it confounds the exposure-response relationship, opening a biasing backdoor path \(E \leftarrow L \rightarrow R\). A concrete example: in an obesity indication, body weight (\(L\)) influences drug exposure (\(E\)) through its effect on pharmacokinetics, while also independently increasing the risk of cardiovascular events (\(R\)). A naïve exposure-response analysis would therefore conflate the drug effect with the background cardiovascular risk driven by body weight.











2.3.3 When to Condition on a Covariate \(L\)?
Whether conditioning on a covariate \(L\) helps, hurts, or is irrelevant depends entirely on its causal role relative to \(D\) and \(R\). Three canonical cases are illustrated below.
Confounder (\(L\) causes both \(D\) and \(R\)): the backdoor path \(D \leftarrow L \rightarrow R\) is open and induces bias. Conditioning on \(L\) blocks this path and is necessary for unbiased estimation of the \(D \to R\) effect.









Collider (\(D\) and \(R\) both cause \(L\)): the path \(D \to L \leftarrow R\) is blocked by default. Conditioning on \(L\) opens this path and introduces bias where none existed. This is a common pitfall — conditioning on a variable that seems relevant can make things worse.









Irrelevant covariate (\(L\) has no causal connection to \(D\) or \(R\)): the path between \(D\) and \(R\) is unaffected whether or not we condition on \(L\). Conditioning on \(L\) neither removes nor introduces bias.











2.3.4 Confounding by Study and Ancestry
A common practice in pharmacometric analyses is to pool data across multiple clinical trials. Within each individual study, randomization ensures that treatment assignment \(D\) is independent of patient covariates. However, when studies are pooled, the variable \(\mathit{Study}\) becomes predictive of \(D\) — because different trials employed different dosing schemes — thereby breaking the exchangeability that randomization had provided within each study.
If patients of Asian ancestry are disproportionately enrolled in certain studies and ancestry independently affects the outcome \(Y\) (whether exposure or response), then the backdoor path \[D \leftarrow \mathit{Study} \rightarrow \mathit{Asian} \rightarrow Y\] is open and the estimate of \(D \to Y\) is confounded. Conditioning on \(\mathit{Asian}\) closes this path and restores exchangeability. Body weight (\(\mathit{WT}\)) and sex (\(\mathit{Sex}\)) play no active causal role in this simplified picture.









After conditioning on \(\mathit{Asian}\), the backdoor path is blocked and all edges along it are no longer biasing.









In practice, the picture is more complex. Body weight (\(\mathit{WT}\)) and sex (\(\mathit{Sex}\)) are also distributed differently across studies and ancestries: Asian patients tend to have lower body weight, and males and females differ systematically in weight. Both \(\mathit{Sex}\) and \(\mathit{Asian}\) independently affect \(Y\) through their influence on pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. The resulting causal structure is shown below.









Four open backdoor paths now exist: \[D \leftarrow \mathit{Study} \rightarrow \mathit{Asian} \rightarrow Y, \qquad
  D \leftarrow \mathit{Study} \rightarrow \mathit{Asian} \rightarrow \mathit{WT} \rightarrow Y,\] \[D \leftarrow \mathit{Study} \rightarrow \mathit{Sex} \rightarrow Y, \qquad
  D \leftarrow \mathit{Study} \rightarrow \mathit{Sex} \rightarrow \mathit{WT} \rightarrow Y.\]
Conditioning on \(\mathit{Asian}\) blocks the first two; conditioning on \(\mathit{Sex}\) blocks the second two. The pair \(\{\mathit{Asian},\, \mathit{Sex}\}\) is therefore a sufficient adjustment set.
\(\mathit{WT}\) might seem a natural covariate to include — it is clinically meaningful, correlated with outcome, and commonly measured. However, \(\mathit{WT}\) is a collider on two otherwise- closed paths: \[D \leftarrow \mathit{Study} \rightarrow \mathit{Asian} \rightarrow \mathit{WT} \leftarrow \mathit{Sex} \rightarrow Y,\] \[D \leftarrow \mathit{Study} \rightarrow \mathit{Sex} \rightarrow \mathit{WT} \leftarrow \mathit{Asian} \rightarrow Y.\] Both arrows point into \(\mathit{WT}\) from different causal directions, so both paths are blocked by default. Conditioning on \(\mathit{WT}\) would open them and introduce a spurious association between \(\mathit{Asian}\) and \(\mathit{Sex}\) — a new source of bias. \(\mathit{WT}\) should therefore not be included in the adjustment set.











2.3.5 Trastuzumab in Gastric Cancer: Conounding due to Cachexia











2.3.6 Immortal Time Bias
Immortal time bias is a form of selection bias that arises when patients are classified into a group only if they survived long enough to satisfy the group-membership criterion. The period between study entry and the moment of classification is immortal time for the members of that group — they cannot, by definition, have died during it. Crediting that person-time to one group but not the other distorts the Kaplan-Meier curves and inflates the apparent survival advantage.
Consider a retrospective analysis of ovarian cancer patients receiving first-line chemotherapy. CA125, a glycoprotein shed by tumor cells, is routinely measured at several cycles during treatment. A common analysis classifies patients as “low CA125” or “high CA125” based on whether their nadir CA125 value falls below a threshold at any point during the observation window. A naïve Kaplan-Meier analysis comparing overall survival between the two groups produces the following figure — a striking but biased result whose origin the DAG below will expose.


Warning: A numeric `legend.position` argument in `theme()` was deprecated in ggplot2
3.5.0.
ℹ Please use the `legend.position.inside` argument of `theme()` instead.









The striking separation between the curves is an artifact of a biased analysis — one that implicitly conditions on a collider. The causal structure is made precise in the following DAG, where \(D\) is the treatment, \(M\) the CA125 level measured at Week 9, \(S_0\) survival to Week 9, \(S_1\) overall survival at end of study, and \(U_F\) unmeasured patient frailty.









\(S_0\) is a collider: both treatment (\(D \to S_0\)) and unmeasured frailty (\(U_F \to S_0\)) influence whether a patient survives to Week 9. On the path \(D \to S_0 \leftarrow U_F\), the collider \(S_0\) blocks all information flow by default — no bias arises from this fork as long as \(S_0\) is left unadjusted.
\(M\), however, can only be observed in patients who survived to Week 9, so any analysis of \(M\) implicitly conditions on \(S_0 = 1\). This is precisely what the Kaplan-Meier analysis above does: by restricting to patients with a measured CA125, it conditions on the collider \(S_0\), opening the otherwise-closed path and inducing a spurious association between \(M\) and \(S_1\). More frail patients (\(U_F\) high) are less likely to reach Week 9; among those who do, the frailty distribution is selectively depleted. Since frailty independently predicts poor long-term survival (\(U_F \to S_1\)), the “low CA125” group — enriched with lower-frailty survivors — appears to have better overall survival regardless of its CA125 value. The KM plot above should therefore not be produced or interpreted as a genuine survival comparison.
This is a general problem in pharmacometric and clinical analyses whenever a subgroup is defined on the basis of post-baseline measurements. Patients classified as “PK-evaluable,” “ADA-positive,” or “biomarker-responders” must by definition have survived long enough — and remained on study long enough — to provide the post-baseline sample. The resulting evaluable population implicitly conditions on an intermediate survival node (\(S_0\)), opening the collider and introducing selection bias into any analysis of overall survival or long-term outcomes.




Textor, Johannes, Benito van der Zander, Mark S Gilthorpe, Maciej Liskiewicz, and George Th Ellison. 2016. “Robust Causal Inference Using Directed Acyclic Graphs: The R Package ’Dagitty’.” Int. J. Epidemiol. 45 (6): 1887–94.

title: 3  Estimands
text:
3.2 Mathematical Representation of Estimands
In order to express estimands mathematically, we need a notational system that distinguishes between what will happen if we let nature take its course, and what would happen if we were to intervene. For the second set of concepts, we will use potential outcome notation. The following exploration in R, adapted from the supplemental material of Rogers, Maas, and Pitarch (2023), is intended to develop intuitions about the differences between conditional distributions of observable quantities on the one hand, and potential outcome distributions on the other.
The fundamental problem of causal inference is that, when it comes to intervening on a single subject or experimental unit, we can only try one thing at a time. This constraint is summarized poetically in the words that Plato attributes to Heraclitus: “… all things move and nothing remains still … you cannot step twice into the same stream.” We can of course return to the same subject, or the same experimental unit, to evaluate a different intervention, but the experimental conditions will never quite be the same. For this reason, the potential outcome distributions associated with any real-world process will only ever be partially observable. In the R-based exploration that follows, we are able to free ourselves from this constraint by working with simulated data. In simulation world, we know all the “what-ifs” that we can’t directly observe in the real world.
For simplicity at the outset, we will consider a scenario with just two levels of treatment, referred to as “control” and “active” and indexed by 0 and 1, and two possible outcomes, corresponding to failure and success, also denoted with 0 and 1. We will simulate 4000 subjects. This number is sufficiently large to make the statistical imprecision in our estimates small in comparison to the treatment effect, so that – for didactic purposes – we can mostly ignore the usual distinction between population and sample, and we can focus exclusively on issues of bias. For each simulated subject, we will set the value of the potential outcome \(Y^0\) (represented in our simulated dataset as Y0 ), corresponding to the outcome that would occur if the given subject receives the control treatment, and the potential outcome \(Y^1\) (represented in our simulated dataset as Y1), corresponding to the outcome that would occur if the given subject receives the active treatment.

set.seed(1)
potential_outcomes <- tibble(
SUBJID = 1:4000,
Y0 = c(rep(1, 1000), rep(0, 1000), rep(1, 500), rep(0, 1500)),
Y1 = c(rep(1, 1000), rep(0, 1000), rep(0, 500), rep(1, 1500))
)
potential_outcomes %>%
group_by(Y0, Y1) %>%
summarise(NSUBJ = n(), .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 4 × 3
     Y0    Y1 NSUBJ
  <dbl> <dbl> <int>
1     0     0  1000
2     0     1  1500
3     1     0   500
4     1     1  1000



potential_outcomes <- potential_outcomes %>%
  mutate(p_ecog_1 = case_when(Y0 + Y1 == 0 ~ 0.75,
                              Y0 + Y1 == 1 ~ 0.5,
                              Y0 + Y1 == 2 ~ 0.25),
         ECOG = rbinom(n(), 1, p_ecog_1),
         NEUTROPHILS = exp(rnorm(n(), 0, 0.5))
         ) %>%
  select(-p_ecog_1)


obs_study <- potential_outcomes %>%
  mutate(
    p_novel = case_when(ECOG == 0 ~ 0.2,
                        ECOG == 1 ~ 0.8),
    A_NAT = rbinom(n(), 1, p_novel),
    TRT = A_NAT,
    YOBS = if_else(TRT == 0, Y0, Y1)
  ) %>%
  select(-p_novel)
obs_study %>% slice_sample(n=10)

# A tibble: 10 × 8
   SUBJID    Y0    Y1  ECOG NEUTROPHILS A_NAT   TRT  YOBS
    <int> <dbl> <dbl> <int>       <dbl> <int> <int> <dbl>
 1   2720     0     1     0       1.23      0     0     0
 2   2398     1     0     0       0.494     0     0     1
 3   1044     0     0     1       0.491     1     1     0
 4   1351     0     0     1       1.37      1     1     0
 5    618     1     1     0       0.551     0     0     1
 6    451     1     1     1       0.627     1     1     1
 7   1076     0     0     1       1.06      1     1     0
 8   3882     0     1     0       0.554     0     0     0
 9    301     1     1     0       0.856     0     0     1
10   3232     0     1     0       1.25      0     0     0


Now that we have a treatment variable and an observed outcome variable, we can investigate the differences between conditional distributions of observed values and potential outcome distributions. This expected value \(E[Y(A=0)]\), a.k.a. \(P(Y(A=0)=1)\) corresponds to this quantity in our code:

obs_study %>% pull(Y0) %>% mean()

[1] 0.375


Contrast that with the expected value \(E[Y | A = 0]\), a.k.a. \(P(Y = 1 | A = 0)\):

obs_study %>% filter(A_NAT == 0) %>% pull(YOBS) %>% mean()

[1] 0.4517413


Comparing the last two quantities tips us off to the following inequality:
\[ E[Y(A=0)] \neq E[Y | A=0] \]
This difference in our unadjusted summaries generally also show up when we look at comparative statistics, such as mean treatment differences. The true (causal) average treatment effect, the “ATE” can be expressed mathematically as
\[ E[ Y(A=1) - Y(A=0) ]. \] The corresponding operation in our code is:

obs_study %>% 
  mutate(ITE = Y1 - Y0) %>% 
  summarise(ATE = mean(ITE)) 

# A tibble: 1 × 1
    ATE
  <dbl>
1  0.25


Compare that to the difference in the observed treatment means. The expected value for this latter quantity can be expressed as:
\[ E[Y | A= 1] - E[Y | A = 0] \]

obs_study %>% 
  group_by(A_NAT) %>% 
  summarise(Ybar = mean(YOBS), .groups = "drop") %>% 
  summarise(UnadjustedEstimateTE = diff(Ybar))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  UnadjustedEstimateTE
                 <dbl>
1               0.0990


We can see that in this case, a naïve analysis would result in a substantial underestimate of the treatment effect. This is because the expected value of our estimate is not equal to the causal quantity of interest:
\[  E[ Y(A=1) - Y(A=0) ] \neq E[Y | A= 1] - E[Y | A = 0] \]
We can also consider several conditional average treatment effects or “CATEs”. For example, the CATEs conditional on baseline ECOG can be expressed mathematically as:
\[ E[ Y(A=1) - Y(A=0) \,|\, \mathit{ECOG}=0] \,\, \mbox{ and } \,\,E[ Y(A=1) - Y(A=0) \,|\, \mathit{ECOG}=1] \] \[ E[ Y(\mathit{Dose}=1) - Y(\mathit{Dose=0}) \,|\, \mathit{ECOG}=0] \,\, \mbox{ and } \,\,E[ Y(A=1) - Y(A=0) \,|\, \mathit{ECOG}=1] \]

obs_study %>% 
  mutate(ITE = Y1 - Y0) %>% 
  group_by(ECOG) %>% 
  summarise(CATE = mean(ITE))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
   ECOG  CATE
  <int> <dbl>
1     0 0.248
2     1 0.252


We can see that these are actually well-approximated by the corresponding conditional distributions in the observable data:

obs_study %>% 
  group_by(A_NAT, ECOG) %>% 
  summarise(Ybar = mean(YOBS), .groups = "drop") %>% 
  group_by(ECOG) %>% 
  summarise(ConditionalEstimateTE = diff(Ybar))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
   ECOG ConditionalEstimateTE
  <int>                 <dbl>
1     0                 0.263
2     1                 0.242


A number of the other variants of causal effects are simply special cases of conditional average treatment effects. For example, the average treatment effect in the treated (“ATT”) is simply the CATE that results from conditioning on being treated.

title: 3  Estimands
text:
3.3 Dose-exposure-response Estimands
A typical development program proceeds by selecting doses primarily based on Phase 2 data, and then confirming the efficacy and safety at the given dose(s) in Phase 3. Whereas hypothetical questions may appropriately play a greater role in earlier stages of development, the late development context gives increasing consideration to directly pragmatic questions about use, “in the wild”. (For example, in early development, the question, “What would have been the efficacy if adherence to the prescribed dosing regimen had been better?” will be relevant if it is possible to achieve better adherence with, e.g., changes in formulation or route of administration or dosing frequency; such hypotheticals become less relevant in later development when the goal confirm that a particular posology achieves acceptable benefit risk. Bartels et al. (2025) examines a hypothetical estimand of this nature.) Late development is therefore a context where treatment policy estimands have special relevance Fleming et al. (2025). Several examples of such estimands for the purpose of dose selection and dose justification in the late development context were considered in Bartels et al. (2026).
The presumed causal structure in Bartels et al. (2026) is summarized in the following DAG. Note that we appear to have broken our own rules, since the graph includes undirected edges (with no arrowheads) between the covariate (“L”) variables. This is just our way of signaling that the variables represented in these three nodes have a joint distribution with a statistical dependence structure that we acknowledge without bothering to explain the causal dependencies that give rise to the statistical dependencies (it turns out that we don’t need to specify that level of detail for the relevant derivations to work).









We now review these scenarios.

3.3.1 Scenario 1: No difference between treatment policy and hypothetical estimands
In the first scenario, we treat dose reduction itself as the endpoint of interest (the idea being that, in this context, a dose reduction signifies a starting dose that was too high), and we proceed as if there are no intercurrent events between the initial dose assignment and dose reductions. Given that assumption, there is no distinction between the treatment policy estimand and the hypothetical estimand (because we can’t even entertain intervening on the intercurrent events if there are no intercurrent events!)









The DAG expresses our assumptions, and our estimand may be expressed as:
\[ E\left[R(D=d) \,\,| \,\, \mathit{ATLL}\right] \] For now we defer the question of how best to estimate this quantity. We will come to that in later chapters in our discussion of adjustment methods such as \(g\)-estimation.


3.3.2 Scenario 2: Forced to choose treatment policy or hypothetical estimand
We now consider a different endpoint, taking platelets at study end as the primary endpoint of interest. In this framing, dose reduction must be considered as an intercurrent event, because such events may occur at times after dose assignment and before measurement of the outcome. We assume the same causal connections as above:









Our treatment policy estimand has the same form as in the previous scenario, but with \(Y\) rather than \(R\) as our outcome:
\[ E\left[Y(D=d) \,\,| \,\, \mathit{ATLL}\right] \]
If our interest were in the hypothetical scenario where dose reductions do not occur, there would be no easy way to represent this on the DAG; instead, a more complex graphical representation, known as a single-world intervention graph (SWIG) could be used. For the time being, we maintain on our focus on the treatment policy estimand, and we can defer the introduction of SWIG notation. We can, however, represent hypothetical estimands mathematically, but expanding our potential outcome notation to signal two interventions: the primary intervention on dose and a hypothetical intervention in which we prevent dose reductions:
\[ E\left[Y(D=d, R=0) \,\,| \,\, \mathit{ATLL}\right] \]


3.3.3 Scenario 3: Special Target Population
In the third scenario, we maintain a focus on platelets as our outcome of interest, but with an eye toward labeling recommendations for special populations, we adjust our target population to be the renally impaired (as an operational definition, we will define this as the subset of the overall ATLL population with creatinine clearance < 60 mL/min). Here our DAG would remain as above, but we now take our estimands to be:
\[ E[Y(D=d) \,\,| ATLL, CRCL < 60] \]

Pharmacol. 14 (1): 68–81.


Bartels, Christian, Yuchen Wang, Jonathan French, and James Rogers. 2026. “Some Common Dose-Exposure-Response Estimands and Conditions for Their Causal Identifiability.” CPT Pharmacometrics Syst. Pharmacol. 15 (2): e70202.
